stemMd:
Reviewer: The museum's new wing was paid for by a company that conceals its emissions data, and the museum knew this when it accepted the gift. The museum has for years urged the public to hold polluters to account. The wing itself is admirable and its programmes reach thousands of schoolchildren. Nevertheless, the museum was wrong to take the money.

Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reviewer's reasoning?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Once a gift has been put to good use, such as the education of schoolchildren, the donor's conduct becomes irrelevant to whether accepting it was proper.

options.label: B
options.textMd: An institution may properly accept a gift whenever the programmes it pays for will benefit many members of the public, whatever the donor's own conduct.

options.label: C
options.textMd: An institution acts wrongly in knowingly taking a benefit from a party that falls short of a standard it urges on the public, however much good the benefit does.

options.label: D
options.textMd: An institution should disclose to the public the source of every gift it receives, together with whatever it knows about the conduct of the donor.

options.label: E
options.textMd: An institution becomes answerable for the conduct of its donors from the moment it accepts a gift, and must then press them to meet its public standards.

explanationMd:
On a justify-the-reasoning question, the winning principle has to license the exact conclusion from the exact premises the arguer relies on. So list them.

- The donor conceals its emissions data.
- The museum **knew** this when it accepted.
- The museum publicly urges others to hold polluters to account.
- The wing does real good.
- Conclusion: accepting was **wrong**.

A principle that justifies this must do two things. It must make the donor's conduct plus the museum's own public stance enough to condemn acceptance, and it must survive the concession that the wing does good — because the reviewer grants that and condemns the museum anyway. The principle holding that an institution acts wrongly in knowingly taking a benefit from a party that falls short of a standard it urges on the public, however much good the benefit does, does both: the trigger is knowingly taking a benefit from a party falling short of the standard the museum urges on the public, and the closing clause, "however much good the benefit does", neutralises the concession.

The check to run on every candidate is: *plug the passage's facts into the principle and see which verdict comes out.* The principle that an institution may properly accept a gift whenever the programmes it pays for will benefit many members of the public yields the opposite verdict here, since the wing's programmes reach thousands of schoolchildren. The principle that a donor's conduct becomes irrelevant once a gift has been put to good use, such as educating schoolchildren, explicitly excuses the museum. The principle that an institution becomes answerable for its donors' conduct from the moment it accepts a gift, and must then press them to meet its standards, concerns duties going forward, not the propriety of accepting, so it never reaches the reviewer's conclusion. The principle requiring disclosure of every gift's source and of what the institution knows about the donor issues a requirement the museum may have met in full; nothing in the passage says the source or the donor's record was hidden.

Also worth noticing is the shape of the reviewer's argument: a concession ("the wing itself is admirable") followed by a conclusion that overrides it. When an argument concedes a benefit and condemns anyway, the principle you need is one that makes the wrongness independent of consequences. Scan the choices for that feature first and the search narrows immediately.

distractorRationale.b: This is a permission keyed to public benefit, and on the passage's own facts the museum qualifies: the wing's programmes reach thousands of schoolchildren, and the principle expressly sets the donor's conduct aside. A principle that would acquit the museum cannot justify the reviewer's verdict that the museum acted wrongly.
distractorRationale.a: This directly excuses the conduct the reviewer condemns, by declaring the donor's behaviour irrelevant once the gift is doing good, and the education of schoolchildren is exactly the good use the passage describes. It is the principle the museum's defenders would invoke, and it catches a reader who selects the choice that echoes the passage's details without checking which side it lands on.
distractorRationale.e: This assigns the museum ongoing duties toward its donors after the gift, whereas the reviewer's charge concerns the single act of accepting. A principle about what an institution must do once it has accepted leaves the propriety of acceptance untouched; if anything it assumes acceptance may go ahead, so it cannot deliver the conclusion the argument reaches.
distractorRationale.d: This imposes a duty of disclosure, and the passage never suggests the museum hid where the money came from or what it knew of the donor; the reviewer plainly knows both. Satisfying a disclosure rule is compatible with having been wrong to accept, so this principle neither condemns nor excuses the conduct at issue.

accessibilityText: A reviewer's argument. A museum knowingly accepted funding for a new wing from a company that conceals its emissions data, although the museum has long urged the public to hold polluters to account; the wing is admirable and serves thousands of schoolchildren; the reviewer concludes the museum was wrong to take the money. The question asks which principle most helps to justify that reasoning. Five answer choices, labelled A through E. No notation, tables or figures appear.

provenance.notes: Original stimulus and choices. Identify-the-principle item built so that the key must both supply the trigger and override an explicit concession about consequences; no real museum, company or donation is referred to. Not derived from any published LSAT item.

review.author: lsat-wave3-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The reviewer's premises are knowing acceptance, a donor failing the standard the museum urges on the public, and the concession that the wing does much good; the principle that knowingly taking benefit from such a party is wrong however much good it does maps onto all three and yields the conclusion. The 'good use makes donor irrelevant' and 'benefit many whatever the donor' principles support the opposite; disclosure and post-acceptance answerability do not address whether taking the money was wrong. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-cue-batch1-run1) reached the same answer: The reviewer's premises are knowing acceptance, a donor who falls short of the standard the museum urges on the public, and conceded good done by the gift; the principle about knowingly taking a benefit from a party below a standard one urges, however much good it does, maps onto each element. The two principles saying good use or public benefit makes acceptance proper support the opposite conclusion; disclosure and becoming answerable afterwards do not establish that taking the money was wrong.]
